hints: Notice the slit in the diagram is a narrow vertical line and the laser spot is centred on it.
Recall that diffraction through a single slit spreads the light mainly at right angles to the long direction of the slit.
Compare a horizontal spread with a vertical spread and decide which is at right angles to the vertical slit.
walkthrough: Look at the diagram: the panel has a narrow vertical slit and the circular cross-section of the laser beam hits the centre of it.
The slit width is narrow and comparable to the wavelength of light, so the light diffracts after passing through rather than forming a small geometric image.
The rule for a single slit is that diffraction spreading is greatest in the direction across the narrow width, which is at right angles to the length of the slit.
Here the slit length is vertical, so the narrow width is horizontal and the diffraction pattern spreads horizontally.
The single-slit pattern has a bright wide central maximum with fainter fringes on either side along the spreading direction, seen as a horizontal band.

options.A: A small dot assumes the light passes straight through with no spreading, which ignores diffraction at the narrow slit.
options.B: A vertical slit diffracts light mainly in the horizontal direction, giving a wide horizontal central maximum on the screen.
options.C: A vertical streak is spreading parallel to the slit, whereas single-slit diffraction spreads at right angles to the slit length.
options.D: A large circular spot suggests uniform spreading in all directions, not the one-dimensional diffraction pattern of a slit.
